newsitem.title: USA: Scripps to buy six dailies, TV station.
newsitem.headline: Scripps to buy six dailies, TV station.

text.p: Flush with cash from the sale of its cable television business last year, E.W. Scripps Co. Monday agreed to pay up to $775 million to buy six daily newspapers and a top-rated TV station to beef up its core operations.

Scripps will pay Harte-Hanks Communications Inc. up to $605 million in stock in a deal meant to be tax free, but it agreed to pay $775 million in cash to Harte-Hanks if tax-free treatment was not feasible. Pending federal legislation would end certain tax-free transactions.

"This is the kind of deal we've been looking for," Scripps President William Burleigh said. "For an attractive price, we're going to greatly increase the geographic diversity of our newspaper division."
The properties include five mid-sized daily newspapers in Texas; one in Anderson, S.C.; KENS-TV in San Antonio, Texas, and a sister radio station, and a chain of Dallas-area weeklies.
Burleigh said KENS-TV "has been one of the industry's strongest franchises for many years."
He said it would be the only station affiliated with Westinghouse Electric Corp.'s CBS network. Its other nine TV stations are affiliated with Walt Disney Co.'s ABC and General Electric Co.'s NBC.

Scripps said the deal would slightly dilute earnings the first year of ownership but would add to earnings by the second or third year. The businesses were projected to produce $65 million in cash flow -- earnings before interest, taxes and other items, in 1998.
Last November, Scripps got out of the cable television business, selling its cable systems to Comcast Corp. for about $1.5 billion.
Analysts said they had expected Scripps to make some acquisitions soon, especially since it was expected to end the year with virtually no long-term debt and flush with cash.
"My concern was where do they go from here," said Dennis McAlpine, an analyst at Josephthal, Lyon & Ross. "Do you put the money into something other than T-bills. It's a very rational deal."
Some analysts said newspapers were still a solid contributor to earnings.
"Newspapers are still a good solid business," said John Morton, who runs his own research firm in Silver Spring, Md.
"They're not rapidly growing in terms of revenues, but they're a reasonably reliable one. That's why people are willing to pay such high multiples to acquire them."
Analysts saw the broadcast acquisition as a plum.

"It's one hell of a (TV) station in San Antonio," said Michael Kupinski at A.G. Edwards. "It's been a ratings leader in the market for the past 20 years. It's extremely well run. It's a nice fit in a good growth market. It's a jewel of an acquisition."
He valued the station at about $180 million.
Analysts said that while Hart-Hanks sought to unload the properties to concentrate on its direct marketing business, a sale was complicated by its insistence on a tax-free deal for its shareholders.
At least one potential buyer, A.H. Belo Corp., had been interested, but changed its mind due to the tax issue, according to Kupinski. A Belo official declined to comment.
Harte-Hanks was concerned that since it has owned the properties for so long and had them at a low value on its books that capital gains taxes would have been high, analysts said.
Scripps stock fell 37.5 cents to $37.875 and Harte-Hanks added $1.25 to $30.25, both on the New York Stock Exchange.
Scripps also said its board authorized the repurchase of up to the maximum number of Class A common shares that could be issued through the Harte-Hanks transaction.
